Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette: Priya was pulling her sedan into the loading lane behind the convenience store on Elm Street when a man stepped out from between two delivery trucks. He did not ask. He pressed something cold against her ribs, told her to keep her hands visible, and ordered her to unlock the glove compartment. She obeyed because her legs had locked, because the voice was low and immediate, because he shifted his weight and she knew hesitation would cost her more. He took her wallet, her phone, and her delivery tablet. He told her to drive away slowly, that he was watching. She did. In the weeks that followed, Priya's mind offered the encounter in fragments. She kept seeing the scuff of the man's boots against the asphalt, the glare of the streetlamp catching metal, the way his jacket zipped halfway up his chest. When she closed her eyes, she heard the sharp crack of his lighter, the metallic click of the lock snapping back, the low rumble of his warning. Some nights, none of that came at all. She would simply jolt awake, her chest tight, her pulse hammering with the exact same terror, though she could not recall a single picture or sound. The memory stayed fixed on the key turning in the ignition, on her own silence. She would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. The guilt sat heavy in her stomach. She stopped answering messages from her cousins in Flushing, stopped going to the community center. She felt cut off, as if a glass wall now separated her from everyone else. At the same time, she told herself over and over that it was fine, that it wasn't really that bad, that she was lucky she walked away. The words felt hollow, but she kept repeating them until the memory blurred. Comfort became impossible. Before walking into any building, Priya's eyes scanned for exits, counting doors, noting which stairwells were locked. She parked her car facing the street, never back in, so she could bolt forward if she needed to. When a delivery courier stood too still near the loading dock, Priya's stomach dropped. She couldn't look at him. She turned her cart around and walked away. At night, she woke at least twice, sitting up in bed to listen for footsteps, to check that the deadbolt was still thrown. Even in her own apartment, with the windows shut and the radiator hissing, her shoulders stayed braced. She could not let go. Her work environment held its own weight. As a delivery driver, she spent her days navigating gridlocked streets and tight alleyways. One Tuesday, a police cruiser pulled up alongside her at an intersection. The officer leaned out, asking for her registration. Priya's breath stopped. Her hands gripped the steering wheel until her knuckles went white. She could not speak. She just nodded, hands trembling, and drove off the moment the light turned green. After that, she stopped driving. She asked her supervisor to switch her to warehouse sorting. When she tried to ride in a coworker's car to visit her sister, her throat closed, her vision tunneled, and she begged to be let out at the first stop. She started taking pills before work, just enough to quiet the noise in her head, just enough to sleep. At twenty-two, Priya walked into the clinic with her coat pulled tight and her eyes fixed on the floor. She had come because the warehouse shelves made her nauseous, because she kept waking up gasping, because the pills were not working anymore. She said she just wanted to know how to stop feeling like the world was always one wrong turn away from collapsing. She hoped, quietly, to be able to drive again. She was most afraid, though, that no matter what she did, she would never be able to stop the bad things from finding her.
